claims.text: Replacing EAM+TI with an MTP+FEP workflow will reduce the computational cost of calculating the TaVCrW melting temperature by more than 80%.
The MTP+FEP workflow will maintain a free-energy error below 0.5 meV/atom.
Achieving the stated accuracy depends on the MTP capturing SRO-induced modifications of the solid-state VDOS.
TaVCrW has a disordered BCC solid phase and a liquid phase relevant to the melting calculation.
The TaVCrW solid exhibits short-range order.
Electronic excitations near the Fermi level may materially affect TaVCrW melting behavior.
A supercell larger than approximately 100 atoms is sufficient to capture SRO clusters and statistically converge the VDOS and phase-space distribution.
Neglecting high-temperature magnetic fluctuations is an acceptable first-order approximation over 2000-2400 K.
SRO clusters generate high-frequency optical structure in the VDOS that the MTP must reproduce as part of the ab initio phase-space distribution.
The high-frequency VDOS features associated with SRO stabilize the solid phase and shift its melting point.
The MTP captures the enthalpic cost of disrupting local SRO, represented by ΔH_DAPB.
EAM-based thermodynamic integration misses SRO-related enthalpy and VDOS effects because of underbinding or overbinding errors involving V and Cr.
Accurate MTP phase-space sampling enables FEP to calculate free-energy differences directly while avoiding the slow convergence of thermodynamic integration.
The MTP+FEP calculation will preserve an SRO stabilization contribution of approximately 2-3 meV/atom.
The predicted melting temperature will differ from the TOR-TILD result by less than 10 K.
TOR-TILD using EAM references and thermodynamic integration is computationally expensive.
The usual GGA-PBE/LDA underbinding and overbinding rules fail for V and Cr at 0 K and may propagate errors into the calculation.
The method is valid only when the supercell statistically represents SRO and the 2000-2400 K range does not activate magnetic physics absent from the MTP.
High-temperature magnetic fluctuations omitted from training could shift the melting point by tens of kelvin.
Insufficient representation of V-Cr local environments in the liquid training data may propagate errors into the MTP predictions.
